newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Settlers agree to remove West Bank caravans.
newsitem.headline: Settlers agree to remove West Bank caravans.

text.p: Jewish settlers agreed to leave a West Bank hilltop they occupied on Friday, ending a tense standoff with police, witnesses said.

They said a settler leader announced a deal had been struck with the government under which the 200 settlers would remove the seven mobile homes from the site on Sunday, in exchange for a meeting to discuss expanding Beit El settlement.

The settlement thrust under the cover of darkness signalled growing pressure on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against an emerging deal with the Palestinians on extending self-rule to the town of Hebron.
"This is a protest action," said Aharon Domb of the Yesha Jewish settlers council during the campaign. "There is a bitter spirit between Yesha and the Prime Minister."
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross met Netanyahu in an effort to close gaps between Israel and the PLO on the Hebron redeployment.
Netanyahu's office said in a statement that no meeting had been scheduled between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, and Ross's contacts with the two sides would continue.
The deal with the settlers was reached after hundreds of Israeli riot police ringed the hilltop near PLO-ruled Ramallah, north of Jerusalem.

Palestinian officials were furious over the settlement bid they said posed a new obstacle to the elusive Hebron deal only two days after an off-duty soldier opened fire on Palestinians in the town's market, wounding seven and raising fears over the future co-existence of the town's 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs.
Arafat aide Ahmed Tibi termed the settlers' moving seven mobile homes onto a West Bank hilltop "a serious threat to the peace process."

Ross has failed in nearly two weeks of intense mediation efforts to persuade Netanyahu and Arafat to seal the long-overdue Hebron accord despite repeated reports they were just hours away from signing.
The United States pressed Israel and the Palestinians to complete the deal, saying protracted negotiations were fuelling instability and the potential for what it called increased terrorist activity.

In Washington, state department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "They have the capacity to make this deal. It's up to them to do it. They are the only ones who can." Burns called the deal, due to be completed nearly one year ago, "long overdue".
Most of Hebron was to be handed over to Palestinians nine months ago under a 1995 Israeli-PLO peace deal but violence and security concerns have held it up.

Palestinian negotiator Jamil al-Tarifi said the main dispute now was a PLO demand that Israel commit itself to target dates for further redeployments after Hebron, mostly in rural areas of the West Bank. These redeployments were already agreed in previous peace deals.
Palestinian officials pointed out Friday's settlement bid was in one of the rural areas Israel was supposed to evacuate in the next stages of the accord.
Netanyahu's top policy adviser, who early on Thursday was predicting a summit within hours, later accused Palestinians of stalling at the final hour to squeeze Israel for concessions.
"Well, it's quite clear the stalling is being done by the Palestinian Authority," said adviser David Bar-Illan.
"The most reasonable guess is that they're doing it because they feel that the situation of no agreement favours them and is detrimental to us," he told Israel Radio.
